title: Uber Builds MCP Gateway to Govern Access to 800+ Servers and 5,000+ AI Agent Tools
gist: Uber built an MCP Gateway spanning 800+ MCP servers and 5,000+ tools that exposes existing HTTP/gRPC/TChannel APIs as agent tools via a registry (control plane) and proxy (data plane), with LLM-generated tool descriptions, owner-gated enablement, tool-level authorization and PII redaction. Commentators note it mirrors decades-old API/GraphQL gateway patterns, and Uber's Omni MCP tackles context bloat via incremental tool discovery.

insights.claim: Uber's MCP Gateway supports more than 800 MCP servers and 5,000 tools, giving AI agents a common layer for discovery, protocol translation, authorization and execution.
insights.speaker: Leela Kumili
insights.so_what: Agent tool sprawl at large enterprises is already in the thousands, creating demand for centralized governance layers.
insights.quote: The platform supports more than 800 MCP servers and 5,000 tools
insights.locator: Uber has built an MCP Gateway

insights.claim: Uber built the gateway to address fragmented integrations, duplicated infrastructure and inconsistent security practices that emerged as AI agent adoption expanded across the company.
insights.speaker: Leela Kumili
insights.so_what: Uncoordinated agent adoption produces integration debt that forces platform consolidation.
insights.quote: addressing fragmented integrations, duplicated infrastructure, and inconsistent security practices as agent adoption expands across the company
insights.locator: Uber has built an MCP Gateway

insights.claim: Uber's gateway exposes existing internal APIs as MCP tools without requiring changes to the underlying services, translating MCP requests into HTTP, gRPC or TChannel calls and converting responses back.
insights.speaker: Leela Kumili
insights.so_what: Wrapping existing APIs rather than rewriting services lowers the cost of making an enterprise agent-ready.
insights.quote: exposes existing APIs as MCP tools without requiring changes to the underlying services

insights.claim: Uber separates an MCP Registry control plane (tool definitions, schemas, ownership, enablement) from a Proxy Gateway that handles runtime execution.
insights.speaker: Leela Kumili
insights.so_what: Classic control-plane/data-plane separation is being re-applied to agent tooling.

insights.claim: Uber's AutoCrawler, built on Cadence, scans internal IDL registries of Protocol Buffers and Thrift schemas, generates MCP-compatible schemas and uses an LLM to write tool descriptions.
insights.speaker: Leela Kumili
insights.so_what: LLMs are being used to bootstrap agent-facing metadata at scale, reducing manual onboarding cost.

insights.claim: Tools newly discovered by Uber's crawler remain disabled until their owning teams review and explicitly enable them, and configuration changes propagate to the data plane without restarts.
insights.speaker: Leela Kumili
insights.so_what: Human-in-the-loop enablement is a governance pattern enterprises adopt to contain agent risk.
insights.quote: Newly discovered tools remain disabled until their owning teams review and explicitly enable them.

insights.claim: Uber's MCP gateway enforces authorization at both server and tool levels and supports redaction of PII and other sensitive data in tool responses; a separate service exchanges internal tokens for third-party tokens for integrations like Jira and Google.
insights.speaker: Leela Kumili
insights.so_what: Security and data redaction for agent tool calls is becoming core infrastructure, a market for gateway/security vendors.
insights.locator: The gateway enforces authorization at both

insights.claim: Loading definitions for thousands of tools into an agent's context is inefficient, so Uber built Omni MCP for incremental discovery where agents search servers, find relevant tools and fetch individual schemas on demand.
insights.speaker: Leela Kumili
insights.so_what: Context-window limits drive a shift from static tool lists to search-based tool retrieval.
insights.quote: loading definitions for thousands of tools into an agent’s context becomes inefficient

insights.claim: Uber's Response Projection lets agents request specific response fields rather than full payloads, and its aifx CLI lets coding agents invoke tools and write results to files for selective inspection.
insights.speaker: Leela Kumili
insights.so_what: Token-economy optimizations are becoming first-class design concerns in agent platforms.

insights.claim: Industry practitioners argue Uber's MCP gateway is essentially the same pattern as API and GraphQL gateways built over decades, implying agent infrastructure reuses established distributed-systems concerns like security, discovery, observability and governance.
insights.speaker: Leela Kumili
insights.so_what: Incumbent API-gateway vendors may be well positioned to capture MCP gateway demand.
insights.quote: Uber's new MCP gateway looks identical to gateways we've built over the decades for APIs and later GraphQL.

insights.claim: A Microsoft CoreAI engineer claims Azure API gateways have long provided this kind of control, describing such gateways as a way to bring order to LLM-induced chaos.
insights.speaker: Leela Kumili
insights.so_what: Cloud hyperscalers can position existing API management products as agent governance layers.
insights.quote: Azure API Gateways has been doing this for a while now. It's a recipe for order to the chaos that LLMs come with.
